Her position was cited during an interview about a possible Bank of Japan rate increase in December, amid above-target inflation, rising wages and yen weakness. No criticism of the bank's competence or institutional threats was reported.

JPN.title: Government guidelines set expectations for BOJ cooperation
JPN.summary: Japan's government approved its annual economic policy guidelines after repeated revisions, particularly to language setting expectations for the Bank of Japan and its cooperation with the government in achieving policy goals. Bloomberg's Molly Smith cited the guidelines in discussing concerns about BOJ independence. The report did not specify a monetary policy direction, institutional changes or threats, and dated approval only to the preceding week.

MEX.title: AMLO calls for lower interest rates in Bloomberg interview
MEX.summary: In a Bloomberg interview in Mexico City, Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador urged the Bank of Mexico to consider growth alongside inflation and said lower interest rates were important to encourage growth. The bank's key rate stood at a decade-high 8.25% amid a slowing economy. He said its caution about inflation was not wrong and explicitly left the rate decision to the central bank.

MEX.title: López Obrador proposes using Banxico SDRs to repay debt
MEX.summary: In 2021, Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador proposed that the Bank of Mexico hand over its IMF special drawing rights to repay debt. Deputy Governor Gerardo Esquivel explained on Twitter that these were reserve assets legally held by the central bank. López Obrador responded by calling Esquivel an “ultratechnocrat” and rigid. The linked report does not establish the intervention’s exact date.

MEX.title: López Obrador attacks Esquivel over SDR explanation
MEX.summary: Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador called Bank of Mexico Deputy Governor Gerardo Esquivel an “ultratechnocrat” and rigid after Esquivel explained on Twitter that IMF special drawing rights were reserve assets legally held by the central bank, countering the president’s proposal to use them to pay debt. The November 10, 2022 report recalled the exchange as occurring in 2021 but provided no exact date.

MEX.title: López Obrador criticizes interest-rate increases at morning conference
MEX.summary: At his Tuesday morning press conference, Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador criticized interest-rate increases pursued by the Bank of Mexico and other central banks to combat inflation, saying the strategy was not ideal because it restrained growth. His remarks came ahead of a Bank of Mexico policy decision, with markets expecting another 75-basis-point increase.

MEX.title: López Obrador calls Esquivel an ultratechnocrat
MEX.summary: Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador publicly called Bank of Mexico deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel an “ultratechnocrat” in 2021, criticizing an official with whom he had previously been close. The linked retrospective does not establish the exact date, a specific policy demand or any threat accompanying the remark.

MEX.title: López Obrador proposes growth objective for Bank of Mexico
MEX.summary: Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador suggested from the National Palace that the Bank of Mexico should also oversee economic growth rather than focus solely on inflation. Recalling the proposal, Deputy Governor Irene Espinosa argued that an explicit growth mandate was unnecessary because price stability supports investment and growth. The report did not specify when the president made the suggestion.

MEX.title: Xochitl Galvez calls for lower interest rates in Bloomberg interview
MEX.summary: In a Bloomberg News interview, Xochitl Galvez, coordinator of Mexico’s opposition Frente Amplio por México and a presidential hopeful, urged the Bank of Mexico to start lowering interest rates to encourage productive investment. She also argued that the strong peso hurt exporters and called for a currency reflecting economic conditions. Coverage reported that the bank was not considering cuts until its inflation objectives were met.

MEX.title: López Obrador sought an advance on Banxico's expected surplus
MEX.summary: According to former Bank of Mexico deputy governor Gerardo Esquivel’s April 28, 2025 column, President Andrés Manuel López Obrador sought an advance in 2020 on an anticipated central-bank operating surplus following the peso’s pandemic depreciation. Esquivel said an unnamed external adviser had suggested the advance was possible, but the governing board adhered to the law and refused. No operating surplus ultimately materialized for that fiscal year.

MEX.title: Sheinbaum urges coordination at Banxico centenary
MEX.summary: At Banco de México’s centenary celebration at the Museo Interactivo de Economía, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum urged closer coordination between the government, central bank and private banks, saying central bank autonomy need not mean a lack of coordination. She also praised the bank’s contribution to stability amid tariffs. Her speech did not establish a monetary policy direction or propose changes to the bank’s mandate or autonomy.

MEX.title: Sheinbaum raises dual mandate discussions
MEX.summary: Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum raised the issue of a dual mandate for Banco de México weeks before its August 25, 2025 centenary celebration, saying she had discussed it with bankers. The report identifies no concrete proposal, specific policy demand or threat to the bank’s autonomy, and does not establish the exact date of her remarks.

MEX.title: López Obrador seeks growth focus in Bloomberg interview
MEX.summary: In a 2019 Bloomberg interview, then-Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador said he wanted Banco de México to consider economic growth as well as inflation. The linked retrospective places his remarks in the debate over a dual mandate but reports no specific legal change, policy-rate demand or threat. The interview’s exact date is not established.

MEX.title: Sheinbaum endorses rate cuts and backs Banxico governor
MEX.summary: At her morning press conference, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum endorsed lower Bank of Mexico interest rates as beneficial for investment and expressed support for Governor Victoria Rodríguez. Speaking before the bank announced its decision, she said she did not know the outcome but considered its March cut correct because headline inflation slowed in April. Later that day, the bank cut its rate by 25 basis points to 6.50% and indicated that it expected to hold that level.

NGA.title: Opposition candidate proposes replacing governor and floating naira
NGA.summary: In an interview reported on January 17 ahead of Nigeria's February 16 presidential election, main opposition candidate Mr Abu Bakr said he would float the naira and appoint a new Central Bank of Nigeria governor if elected. Asked about replacing the governor, he replied, “If I became president, why not?” but qualified this with “If his term expires.” He said the governor had not pursued the right central bank policy.

NGA.title: Tinubu alleges currency controversy is sabotaging his campaign
NGA.summary: Bola Tinubu, the ruling All Progressives Congress presidential candidate and an ally of Nigeria's president, alleged that unnamed people were using controversy over the Central Bank of Nigeria's currency swap to sabotage his campaign. The allegation came amid cash shortages and disruption ahead of elections; the report attributed no specific policy demand or threat to Tinubu.

NGA.title: Ruling-party governors warn president over cash shortage
NGA.summary: Governors from Nigeria’s ruling All Progressives Congress warned the president that voters unable to obtain enough cash would blame the party for the Central Bank of Nigeria’s chaotic currency-swap rollout and that the party would lose at the polls. The warning came amid cash shortages ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections; no specific policy demand or threat against bank officials was reported.

NLD.title: Finance minister proposes shorter DNB presidential terms
NLD.summary: Caretaker finance minister Ilko Heijnen proposed shortening Netherlands Bank presidents’ terms from seven to five years, arguing that lengthy service risks organizational stagnation and shorter terms would allow earlier renewal. Outgoing president Klaas Knot opposed the proposal, warning that shorter tenure could prevent Dutch central bankers from attaining influential international positions. The report also noted concerns that shorter terms could increase political pressure on appointments and indirectly on monetary policy.

NLD.title: Finance ministry pushes outsider appointment to change DNB supervisory culture
NLD.summary: Ahead of Klaas Knot’s appointment as president of De Nederlandsche Bank in 2011, the Dutch Finance Ministry pushed for a new face rather than an expected internal candidate. According to the retrospective account, the ministry considered the bank’s financial-crisis performance inadequate and wanted the appointment to signal a change in supervisory culture. Knot was appointed in that context; the precise date of the ministry’s intervention is not established.

NLD.title: Minister announces less stringent anti-money-laundering approach
NLD.summary: In a May 2025 letter to Parliament, Minister Heijne announced a less stringent anti-money-laundering approach, saying requirements governing banks’ checks had gone too far. Banks would have to supply substantially less information under the revised framework overseen by De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB). The intervention concerned regulatory compliance rather than monetary policy; the exact date of the letter is not established.

NOR.title: Solberg calls for transparency about Tangen's investments
NOR.summary: Erna Solberg said incoming oil fund chief Nikolai Tangen should be transparent about his investments, amid discussion of disclosure and arrangements with Norges Bank for handling his financial interests. Tangen reportedly said he had disclosed his fund holdings to the bank and would discuss reporting and management arrangements with it.

NOR.title: Parliamentary hearing scrutinizes Tangen appointment
NOR.summary: Norway’s parliamentary finance committee held a hearing scrutinizing Norges Bank’s appointment of Nikolai Tangen to lead the oil fund. Politicians questioned whether arrangements separating his retained AKO Capital interests from the fund adequately prevented conflicts of interest. Governor Øystein Olsen repeatedly had to explain changes to the bank’s ethical rules allowing Tangen to retain holdings. Norges Bank and Tangen maintained that the arrangements prevented conflicts.

NOR.title: Government requires deputy governor to resign over security risk
NOR.summary: The Norwegian government reportedly required a Norges Bank deputy governor responsible for oversight of the sovereign wealth fund to leave immediately over a perceived security risk linked to his Chinese wife living in China. He resigned on December 4, 2020. The intervention concerned his tenure, not monetary policy.

NOR.title: Rødt warns Stoltenberg could raise rates to prove independence
NOR.summary: Following Jens Stoltenberg’s appointment as Norges Bank governor, Norway’s Rødt party reportedly expressed concern that he might raise interest rates to demonstrate his independence rather than on monetary-policy grounds. The report did not establish an explicit demand for a particular rate path or any threat against his tenure or the bank’s autonomy.

NOR.title: Stoltenberg welcomes rate cut on Instagram
NOR.summary: Jens Stoltenberg welcomed Norges Bank’s interest-rate cut in an Instagram statement following its September 18 decision, saying there was room for rate cuts in Norway. His statement supported monetary easing without criticizing the bank or making threats.

NOR.title: Ministry requests Norges Bank input into monetary-policy mandate review
NOR.summary: As part of a monetary-policy mandate review due to finish the following autumn, the ministry asked Norges Bank to share its experience under the current mandate, examine how monetary policy responds to international supply-side shocks, and help organize a scientific conference in early March. Bank official Ole Christian Bech-Moen said the bank was preparing supporting analyses but would not anticipate its conclusions. The request specified no policy direction or proposed mandate change.

NOR.title: Government retains monetary-policy framework
NOR.summary: Norway’s government concluded on Friday that Norges Bank’s monetary-policy framework would remain unchanged. The interview described this as retaining priority for fighting inflation without defining an unemployment threshold at which the bank should place greater weight on employment. No threat to officials’ tenure or institutional autonomy was reported.

NZL.title: Government directs RBNZ to curb overheated housing market
NZL.summary: The New Zealand government directed the Reserve Bank of New Zealand to curb the overheated housing market, giving it a mandate to keep housing affordable. Reports linked rising New Zealand bond yields to the possibility that the direction could require higher official interest rates. Subsequent commentary questioned how the bank could restrain housing prices without harming an economy recovering from the COVID recession.

NZL.title: Foreign ministry rebukes RBNZ governor for signing Powell support statement
NZL.summary: New Zealand's foreign ministry rebuked Reserve Bank of New Zealand Governor Anna Breman for signing a joint statement supporting Jerome Powell and central bank independence without first consulting politicians. The linked report describes criticism of her participation, but identifies no monetary policy demand or threat to her tenure or the bank's mandate.

POL.title: Polish president proposes using central bank gold profits for defence
POL.summary: Polish President Nawrocki proposed that the National Bank of Poland sell and immediately repurchase gold to realise accounting profits for transfer to the state budget for defence spending, while preserving its gold holdings. Supported by the central bank governor, the proposal was presented as an alternative to EU defence loans worth roughly €43 billion. Prime Minister Donald Tusk opposed the plan, while analysts cited in the report questioned whether it could raise a comparable amount.

RUS.title: Putin’s chief economic adviser blames central bank for ruble decline
RUS.summary: Following the ruble’s fall to roughly one US cent, President Vladimir Putin’s chief economic adviser publicly blamed the Bank of Russia for the depreciation. The report gives no specific policy demand or exact date for the criticism. The bank attributed the decline to government war spending, reduced foreign trade and a labour shortage; it raised its key rate by 3.5 percentage points to 12% and halted domestic foreign-currency purchases.

RUS.title: Putin urges compromise on interest rates at Moscow congress
RUS.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin urged a compromise between businesses and the Bank of Russia in a Moscow congress speech reported in Russian media the previous day. He said interest rates should not become too high, pushing against further increases from 21% without announcing a takeover of monetary policy. Governor Elvira Nabiullina reportedly responded that further increases were not set in stone and would need reassessment.

RUS.title: Putin signals support for lower interest rates
RUS.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin hinted earlier in the week of June 20, 2025, that he supported lower Bank of Russia interest rates to revive economic growth. His signal came amid recession risks and high business borrowing costs, with persistent inflation keeping rates elevated.

RUS.title: Putin calls for a key interest rate cut
RUS.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin recently advocated cutting the Bank of Russia's key interest rate to support the weakening economy ahead of a closely watched leadership meeting. The June 19, 2026 report framed the forthcoming decision as a test of central-bank independence but did not specify when Putin made the statement.

TUR.title: Removal of Turkey's central bank governor
TUR.summary: President Erdogan dismissed Turkish central bank governor Murat Cetinkaya on Saturday, July 6, ahead of the July 25 policy meeting. Investor commentary linked the removal to Erdogan's desire for larger interest-rate cuts and warned that it undermined the bank's independence and credibility. The lira fell nearly 3% at Monday's opening, and several banks subsequently abandoned bullish lira recommendations.

TUR.title: Erdogan urges lawmakers to support his interest-rate policy
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan reportedly urged lawmakers to support the government's economic policies, including his view that higher interest rates cause inflation, reinforcing his preference for lower rates at the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. The report came ahead of the bank's July 25 policy meeting and amid coverage of the governor's dismissal.

TUR.title: Erdogan promises significantly lower interest rates by year-end
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan promised significantly lower interest rates and single-digit inflation by year-end. Reported about a week after his removal of the central bank governor, the promise reinforced expectations that the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey's new leadership would cut rates substantially.

TUR.title: Erdogan fires central bank governor over rate-cut disagreement
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan fired the governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey in 2019 following a disagreement over the pace and depth of interest-rate cuts. The September 24, 2020 report recalled the dismissal as context for the bank's constrained room to raise rates against Erdogan's preference for low interest rates. It did not establish the dismissal's exact date.

TUR.title: Erdogan fires Turkey's central bank governor
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan fired the central bank governor and appointed Naci Agbal as his replacement amid a sustained decline in the lira. The FT reported that Erdogan had received briefings about the worsening economic situation and was unhappy. His son-in-law resigned as finance minister a day later. The departures were reported as potentially signaling a major economic-policy shift, but the dismissal itself established no specific monetary-policy demand.

TUR.title: Turkish president fires central bank governor after rate increase
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed central bank governor Naci Agbal after a larger-than-expected two-percentage-point interest-rate increase intended to curb inflation. He appointed academic Sahap Kavcioglu, who had advocated lower rates and expressed the view that higher rates increase inflation. The overnight weekend dismissal made Kavcioglu Turkey’s fourth governor in less than two years and was followed by sharp falls in the lira and Turkish stocks. The linked reports do not establish the precise dismissal date.

TUR.title: Erdogan dismisses three central bank rate-setting committee members
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed three members of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s rate-setting committee in a midnight decree. Bloomberg reported that the dismissals removed members who opposed his call for continued interest-rate cuts despite high inflation. The lira fell to a record low against the dollar following the dismissals.

TUR.title: Erdogan defends low-rate policy in speech
TUR.summary: In a speech earlier in the week of November 24, 2021, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan defended low interest rates as supporting growth and employment, arguing that higher rates would dampen growth rather than curb inflation. His remarks reinforced pressure on the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey to lower rates despite high inflation and a sharply falling lira. The linked reports do not establish the speech's exact date or identify a threat attached to it.

TUR.title: Erdogan replaces central bank head with low-rate ally
TUR.summary: In March 2021, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed the governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and replaced him with a political ally more supportive of lower interest rates. The linked reporting says the dismissal occurred in the middle of the night, a couple of days after the governor raised rates to control inflation, but does not establish the exact date.

TUR.title: Erdogan pledges to lift the scourge of interest rates
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan asserted, in remarks presented in a Reuters translation, that interest rates cause inflation and pledged to lift the 'scourge of interest rates' from people's backs. Dismissing contrary arguments, he advocated lower rates, opposing Turkish central bank governors' preference for rate increases to control inflation.

TUR.title: Erdogan pledges further rate cuts citing Islamic teachings
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan pledged further interest-rate cuts on Sunday, citing Islamic teachings, and said Turkey would not abandon its economic model based on lower borrowing costs and a cheaper currency. His remarks pressed the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey toward further easing despite its indication after the previous week's rate cut that room for additional cuts was limited. Reports linked his pledge to a new record low for the lira.

TUR.title: Erdogan dismisses central bank governor over rate increases
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed the central bank governor in March 2021, reportedly because he had raised interest rates too quickly for Erdogan’s liking. The reporting describes him as the last relatively independent governor and the third removed within two years; his replacement implemented Erdogan’s preferred low-interest-rate policy. The linked stories do not establish the exact dismissal date.

TUR.title: Erdogan pledges continued interest rate cuts
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said in remarks reported by the Associated Press in October 2022 that interest rates would keep falling for as long as he remained president, adding, "No one should give us advice on this subject." His statement pressed for continued easing by Turkey's central bank despite official inflation of 83 percent. The linked report does not establish the exact date of his remarks.

TUR.title: Opposition campaign questions missing foreign-exchange reserves
TUR.summary: Turkey’s political opposition campaigned to ask where $120–128 billion in foreign-exchange reserves had gone after reserves were spent, challenging the handling of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s reserves and demanding accountability. A November 23, 2022 broadcast recalled the campaign as having begun one to two years earlier and having made reserve depletion a political issue, without establishing an exact date.

TUR.title: Opposition program pledges central bank independence and an end to protected deposits
TUR.summary: Turkey’s opposition parties announced a comprehensive policy roadmap pledging to restore the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s independence and reverse the existing monetary policy framework. They proposed ending renewals of exchange-rate-protected deposit accounts and closing the accounts as they matured. The reported pledges did not establish an explicit interest-rate direction.

TUR.title: Central bank law amended to prohibit Treasury advances
TUR.summary: During a February 7, 2023 Bloomberg HT broadcast on earthquake reconstruction funding, a commentator recalled a historical amendment to Turkey’s central bank law explicitly prohibiting short-term advances to the Treasury, an authority available before the 2001 crisis. The commentator said the statutory prohibition prevented subsequent Treasury borrowing through that channel, citing it as an example of binding legal restrictions on resource use. The amendment’s exact date was not established.

TUR.title: Erdoğan pledges further cuts from 9 percent interest rate
TUR.summary: In a statement in early February 2023, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said that interest rates, then at 9 percent, would be lowered further. A February 23 broadcast ahead of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey's meeting cited his pledge as one reason for expectations of another rate cut. The linked report does not establish the exact date of his statement.

TUR.title: Erdoğan pledges continued low interest rates while in office
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said in a weekend statement that low-interest-rate policies would continue while he remained in office. Broadcasts on April 24–26, 2023 cited the pledge when contrasting his alliance’s monetary-policy stance with the opposition’s proposed return to orthodox policies, and described him as ruling out rate increases. The intervention advocated continuity in the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s low-rate policy; no personnel or institutional threat was reported. The precise statement date is not established.

TUR.title: Nebati rules out interest-rate increases
TUR.summary: Nebati stated that there would definitely be no interest-rate increase, opposing a shift toward tighter policy at the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. His statement was recalled during Bloomberg HT's May 12 broadcast in a discussion of whether monetary policy would change if the incumbent government remained in power.

TUR.title: Erdoğan pledges continued low interest rates in CNN interview
TUR.summary: In a CNN interview cited by a May 22 broadcast, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said interest rates would remain low and no change to the existing policy framework should be expected. Advocating continuity in the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s low-rate policy, he defended the economic program as delivering positive results and said further gains would follow.

TUR.title: Erdoğan reaffirms low interest rates after runoff victory
TUR.summary: After winning Turkey's presidential runoff on May 28, 2023, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan insisted that he would keep interest rates low despite inflation exceeding 40%, reaffirming pressure for low-rate policy at the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. The report does not establish the precise date of his statement.

TUR.title: Erdoğan calls high interest rates the mother of all evil
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan called high interest rates "the mother of all evil," condemning higher rates and expressing a preference for looser monetary policy at Turkey's central bank. The May 30, 2023 report recalled the statement as having been made a few years earlier but did not establish its exact date.

TUR.title: Erdogan denounces interest rates as evil
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called interest rates the "mother and father of all evil," expressing opposition to high rates in the context of pressure on the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. The retrospective report links his preference for lower rates to his belief that higher borrowing costs increase inflation, but does not date this particular statement.

TUR.title: Erdogan says central bank must answer to him
TUR.summary: In a statement recalled as occurring in 2018, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey would have to answer to him, asserting presidential control over monetary policy. The intervention came amid his opposition to high interest rates and the bank's rate increases to counter inflation. The linked account does not establish the statement's exact date.

TUR.title: Erdogan fires central bank governor over high rates
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed the central bank governor because interest rates were too high for his liking, according to a retrospective account published on June 7, 2023. The account places this first of three governor dismissals after Erdogan began asserting greater control over economic policy in 2018, but does not establish its exact date. The dismissal reflected his preference for lower interest rates, contrary to the bank's earlier rate increases to counter inflation.

TUR.title: Erdogan dismisses another central bank governor
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed a second governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey after his initial governor dismissal. The story recalls the removal in the context of his pressure for lower interest rates but provides no date, governor’s name or further particulars about this dismissal.

TUR.title: Erdogan dismisses a third central bank governor
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed a third governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, according to a retrospective account of his pressure for lower interest rates. The story places the dismissal within his opposition to high rates but provides no date, governor's name or further particulars about this removal.

TUR.title: President signals permission for interest-rate increases
TUR.summary: Turkey’s president made remarks that markets interpreted as opening the way for an interest-rate increase by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey ahead of its next Monetary Policy Committee meeting. In Bloomberg HT’s June 15 discussion, a commentator understood the remarks as granting some permission to raise rates. The reporting establishes no specific rate demand, criticism of bank officials or threat.

TUR.title: Yılmaz calls for central bank alignment with government objectives
TUR.summary: Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz said interest rates were technical instruments for the central bank to use, while stressing that the bank should pursue objectives aligned with the government. He also supported gradually winding down exchange-rate-protected deposits as lira assets became more attractive. His reported remarks did not specify an interest-rate direction or threaten institutional changes.

TUR.title: Erdogan dismisses central bank chief after rate increases
TUR.summary: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan dismissed Turkey’s central bank chief in 2021, only months into the governor’s tenure after he began raising interest rates. The report attributed the dismissal to Erdogan’s opposition to high interest rates, recalling it as context for uncertainty about his tolerance of renewed monetary tightening in 2023. The linked story does not establish the dismissal’s exact date.

TUR.title: Three central bank deputy governors replaced
TUR.summary: Turkish authorities removed Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey deputy governors Emrah Şener, Taha Çakmak and Mustafa Duman, replacing them with Osman Cevdet Akçay, Fatih Karahan and Hatice Karahan. The reshuffle changed the bank’s monetary-policy leadership, but the reports establish no explicit policy demand or reason for the removals. Commentators welcomed the appointments as potentially strengthening credibility and market confidence.

TUR.title: Erdogan calls high interest rates the mother and father of all evil
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called high interest rates the "mother and father of all evil," condemning high-rate monetary policy and advocating lower rates. The August 25, 2023 report recalled this undated earlier statement as context for the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey's subsequent shift toward tightening.

TUR.title: Erdoğan endorses continued monetary tightening in medium-term program speech
TUR.summary: In a speech following the medium-term program announcement, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan endorsed continuing tight monetary policy for a while longer, supporting the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s tightening course. Subsequent discussions described his backing as strengthening policy credibility, continuity and coordination with the economic administration, while noting uncertainty arising from his simultaneous insistence on maintaining growth. No threats or institutional changes were reported.

TUR.title: Minister calls for increased central bank reserves
TUR.summary: In a Bloomberg HT discussion, a commentator attributed to a Turkish minister a call to increase the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s reserves. The discussion concerned Turkey’s external financing needs and reportedly negative net reserves excluding swaps. No specific occasion, reserve-building mechanism or monetary-policy direction was identified for the minister’s statement.

TUR.title: Presidential-system reform centralizes central-bank appointment powers
TUR.summary: Under Turkey’s presidential government system, an institutional reform abolished the joint-decree procedure for appointing and dismissing the central-bank governor, placing these decisions with the president. In a November 27, 2023 broadcast, commentators described the change as a structural constraint on the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s independence. The broadcast did not establish when the reform occurred.

TUR.title: Minister signals review of exporters’ mandatory foreign-exchange sales
TUR.summary: An unnamed minister said the requirement for exporters to sell 40 percent of their foreign-exchange proceeds to the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey would be reviewed, according to a broadcast discussion. The discussion linked a possible relaxation to reserve accumulation and noted that an additional 30 percent requirement associated with rediscount financing had already been removed. Commentators anticipated gradual relaxation rather than immediate abolition; no specific reduction or timetable was established by the minister’s reported remarks.

TUR.title: Erdogan appoints Karahan after Erkan resigns
TUR.summary: President Recep Tayyip Erdogan appointed deputy governor Fatih Karahan to lead Turkey’s central bank late on Friday after Hafize Gaye Erkan requested to leave her post. Her resignation followed weeks of unverified allegations that her father exercised an unofficial role at the bank and that she had difficulties with senior staff. The reports do not establish that Erdogan ordered her departure or demanded a policy change. Karahan subsequently signalled continuity in the existing anti-inflation programme.

TUR.title: CHP challenges decree-law changes to central bank appointments
TUR.summary: Turkey’s opposition Republican People’s Party applied to the Constitutional Court in 2018 to annul provisions of decree-law No. 703, including the removal of the rule appointing the central bank governor through the Council of Ministers for five years. The exact filing date is not established. The court ruled on December 7, 2023, with reasons published June 4, 2024, that the challenged changes required legislation rather than a decree-law; the report described the ruling as procedural, not a rejection of presidential appointment authority.

TUR.title: Government shifts exchange-rate-protected deposit costs to central bank
TUR.summary: An expert speaking on Bloomberg HT on July 24, 2024 recalled that the Turkish government had shifted the costs of exchange-rate-protected deposits to the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey after they became an overwhelming budget burden. The expert characterized this as requiring the bank to pay through money creation and criticized the risks the arrangement created for citizens. The date of the government’s intervention was not established.

TUR.title: President advocates rate reductions in aircraft remarks
TUR.summary: A November 22 Bloomberg HT broadcast described the Turkish president’s remarks aboard an aircraft as conveying that interest-rate reductions were necessary. Commentators discussed those remarks alongside signals from the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey that easing might be approaching. The story did not specify when the president made the remarks or report any associated threat.

TUR.title: Erdoğan pledges interest-rate reductions in 2025
TUR.summary: In remarks made over the weekend before December 30, 2024, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan declared that interest rates would definitely begin falling and that 2025 would be a signal year for reductions, advocating easing by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey. While describing lower inflation as the economic programme’s priority, he argued that interest rates must fall for inflation to fall. The linked report does not establish the exact day of his remarks.

TUR.title: Şimşek links inflation success to exchange-rate restraint
TUR.summary: In an interview with Ali Can Türkoğlu reported during the week of May 2, 2025, Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek indicated that the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey needed to restrain exchange-rate depreciation to help meet the inflation objective. He expressed confidence that inflation would remain within the bank’s forecast range, citing weak domestic demand, limited exchange-rate pass-through and falling commodity prices. The exact interview date is not established.

TUR.title: Zeybekçi warns tight conditions prevent production and investment
TUR.summary: Former minister and AK Party economic figure Nihat Zeybekçi warned that prevailing tight conditions prevented Turkey’s real sector from producing and investing. His remarks were cited by a guest on Bloomberg HT’s May 9 broadcast discussing the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s monetary tightening; no specific date for his original remarks was provided.

TUR.title: Nihat Zeybekci criticizes interest rates as incompatible with production and investment
TUR.summary: Former minister and AK Party economic policymaker Nihat Zeybekci publicly challenged prevailing interest rates, invoking his own experience as a businessman and saying the real sector could not produce or invest at those rates. His remarks advocated lower rates in the context of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey's tight monetary policy. The May 23 broadcast recalled the intervention as having already been discussed the previous week, but did not establish its exact date.

TUR.title: President announces expansion of investment advance loans
TUR.summary: Turkey’s president announced an expansion of investment-committed advance loans from 300 billion to 500 billion lira, widening targeted credit under the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey’s programme. The June 19 broadcast reported that the announcement occurred the previous day and described the loans as supporting large investments in selected sectors intended to reduce imports through import substitution. No criticism of bank officials or institutional threats was reported in this intervention.

TUR.title: Erdoğan calls interest rates the mother and father of all evil
TUR.summary: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan called interest rates the “mother and father of all evil,” expressing opposition to high rates in the context of political pressure on Turkey’s central bank. An August 2, 2025 discussion recalled the statement while discussing central-bank independence, but did not establish when Erdoğan made it.

TUR.title: Turkish president replaced central bank chiefs based on loyalty
TUR.summary: In a retrospective comparison with Donald Trump's efforts to politicize the Federal Reserve, The Indicator described Turkey's president as hiring and firing central bank chiefs based on loyalty. The report presented these personnel changes as an example of political control over monetary institutions, but did not establish their dates or identify a specific policy demand.

TUR.title: Erdogan removes central bank chief over monetary-policy disagreement
TUR.summary: In a historical comparison broadcast on January 26, 2026, DS Vandaag recounted how Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan removed the head of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey and installed his own appointee because he wanted interest-rate policy conducted according to his preferences. The account did not identify the dismissed governor, date the removal or specify the policy direction Erdogan demanded.

USA.title: Trump calls Federal Reserve crazy after stock-market plunge
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump blamed the Federal Reserve for a sharp US stock-market decline and said it had gone crazy. His criticism followed a fall of more than 3% in the Dow Jones amid interest-rate expectations. The report identifies no specific policy demand or threat.

USA.title: Trump calls Fed his biggest threat in Fox Business interview
USA.summary: In a Tuesday-night Fox Business Network interview, President Donald Trump called the Federal Reserve his “biggest threat,” saying it was raising interest rates too fast and expressing dissatisfaction with Chair Jay Powell. He acknowledged the Fed's independence and said he did not speak to Powell. Minutes released the following day indicated policymakers still contemplated further rate increases.

USA.title: Trump criticizes his choice of Powell as Fed chair
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump criticized Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, whom he had appointed, saying on Monday that he was not even a little happy with his choice of Jay. The reported remarks expressed dissatisfaction without an explicit policy demand or tenure threat. The story subsequently reported Powell signaling in New York that interest rates could rise more slowly.

USA.title: Trump urges Fed to avoid a rate increase and heed markets
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump urged the Federal Reserve not to raise interest rates ahead of its December meeting, warning officials against making further mistakes and telling them to feel the market rather than rely on meaningless numbers. Despite his criticism, the Fed raised rates by 0.25 percentage points on December 19 to a 2.25–2.5% range. Chair Jerome Powell said political considerations had played no role.

USA.title: Trump criticizes monetary tightening in mid-July tweet
USA.summary: In a mid-July tweet, U.S. President Donald Trump criticized Federal Reserve monetary tightening, saying the United States should not be penalized for doing well and that tightening hurt everything his administration had done. His comments opposed tighter policy and portrayed it as damaging the administration’s achievements. The linked report does not establish the tweet’s exact date.

USA.title: Trump calls Fed the economy's only problem in Christmas Eve tweet
USA.summary: In a Christmas Eve tweet, US President Donald Trump called the Federal Reserve the economy's only problem, saying it lacked a feel for markets and did not understand necessary trade wars, strong dollars or Democratic shutdowns over borders. The criticism followed a Bloomberg report that he had discussed firing Fed Chair Jerome Powell, but the tweet itself made no removal threat or explicit policy demand.

USA.title: Trump contrasts current rates with prior administration's zero rates
USA.summary: In a January 8, 2019 tweet, US President Donald Trump contrasted zero interest rates under the previous administration with current rates and suggested he could achieve more with similarly low rates. The broadcast characterized the tweet as continued criticism of the Federal Reserve; the intervention supported lower rates without an explicit threat.

USA.title: Toomey warns against deliberate inflation overshooting
USA.summary: During Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell’s biannual Senate Banking Committee testimony, Republican Senator Pat Toomey questioned a possible shift to average inflation targeting. He warned against deliberately allowing inflation above the Fed’s two percent target to offset earlier undershooting, saying inflation had historically been harder to control. His objection came as the Fed reviewed its monetary policy framework.

USA.title: Crapo raises concerns about QE and balance-sheet size
USA.summary: During Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell’s biannual Senate Banking Committee testimony, Republican Senator Mike Crapo expressed concern about quantitative easing and the size of the Fed’s balance sheet, questioning its future reduction. Powell discussed estimates of banks’ reserve needs and an additional reserve buffer, providing indications of where balance-sheet reduction could end without announcing a specific end date.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Powell’s rate increases and strong dollar
USA.summary: President Donald Trump criticized Federal Reserve Chairman Jay Powell as someone who “likes raising rates” and said the U.S. economy was doing well despite the central bank’s actions. In remarks reported on March 4, Trump said he wanted a strong dollar, but not one so strong that it hindered U.S. dealings with other nations and its ability to win their business.

USA.title: Trump calls for lower US interest rates
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump called for lower US interest rates. His demand was reported in an April 8 broadcast discussing DNB Markets’ Norwegian forecasts and whether lower rates abroad would limit further Norges Bank increases. An April 11 discussion also referenced his recent rate-cut comments, noting no apparent indication that they had influenced Federal Reserve communications.

USA.title: Trump proposes loyalists for Federal Reserve board
USA.summary: President Donald Trump proposed Stephen Moore and Herman Cain for Federal Reserve governor positions. An April 10 report portrayed the selection of Trump loyalists as an effort to bring the Fed under his control, without identifying a specific policy demand or institutional change. By April 15, several Republican senators reportedly indicated that Cain might not secure Senate confirmation.

USA.title: Trump calls for renewed quantitative easing
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump called for renewed Federal Reserve quantitative easing, described as QE4, alongside interest-rate cuts. An April 11 broadcast referred to the QE call as occurring in the previous week but provided no exact date. Economist Simon French said Fed watchers had looked for a response in the bank's communications but found no indication that it had taken up Trump's demands.

USA.title: Trump blames Fed for lower stock market
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump attacked the Federal Reserve in a tweet, claiming stocks would be 5,000 to 10,000 points higher and US growth would be 4% without its actions. He said the Fed should have eased rather than tightened monetary policy, blaming its judgement for weaker market and economic performance.

USA.title: White House explores alternatives to Fed nominees
USA.summary: White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow said the administration was discussing alternative candidates to President Donald Trump's Federal Reserve picks, Herman Cain and Stephen Moore, as Republican support declined. Kudlow said Cain should decide for himself whether to withdraw from the selection process. The report established no monetary-policy demand, demand for resignation or proposed change to the Fed's institutional autonomy.

USA.title: Trump tweets demand for one-point Fed rate cut and bond purchases
USA.summary: In a series of tweets, US President Donald Trump urged the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates by one percentage point and resume bond purchases. He praised China's economic stimulus and criticized the Fed for raising rates despite low inflation, claiming that his proposed easing would make the US economy take off 'like a rocket.'

USA.title: Larry Kudlow calls for half-point Fed rate cut
USA.summary: White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow called for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates by half a percentage point. The report contrasted his proposal with President Trump's demand for a full-percentage-point reduction, twice the cut Kudlow advocated.

USA.title: Trump calls for Federal Reserve interest-rate cuts
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump called for the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates, according to a May 2 broadcast. Fed Chairman Jay Powell pushed back, saying the existing policy stance was appropriate, inflation would rebound and the economy did not need fresh central-bank support. The report did not specify when Trump made the call.

USA.title: Trump urges Fed to match Chinese stimulus to help win trade dispute
USA.summary: In morning tweets on May 14, 2019, US President Donald Trump urged the Federal Reserve to match China's monetary stimulus by pumping money into the system to offset the trade war's effects and help the United States win the dispute. He said it would be “game over” if the Fed did so, while indicating he still wanted a trade deal with China. Related coverage quoted New York Fed President John Williams warning that tariffs could raise inflation and hurt growth and supply chains.

USA.title: Trump laments lack of control over Fed policy
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump lamented his lack of China-style control over Federal Reserve policy. The report did not identify the occasion, specify a rate demand, or describe any threat or proposal to change the Fed's autonomy.

USA.title: Wilbur Ross criticizes Fed's inflation assumptions and rate increases
USA.summary: In remarks to Bloomberg Television, US Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross criticized Federal Reserve staff economists for wrongly assuming that falling unemployment necessarily generates inflation. He argued that this mistaken premise had led to unwarrantedly aggressive interest-rate increases, described the December increase as at best premature, and urged the Fed to reconsider it.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Fed chair's job performance
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve chair for not doing his job properly. Two June 18, 2019 discussions placed the remarks a couple of days earlier without establishing an exact date. Commentators interpreted the criticism as aggressive pressure that might encourage lower interest rates, but this statement contained no explicit policy demand or dismissal threat.

USA.title: White House examines legality of demoting Powell
USA.summary: According to sources reported by Bloomberg, White House legal officials examined in February 2019 whether Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell could be demoted while remaining a governor, following President Trump's remarks about firing him. Officials reportedly weighed the implications and concluded that firing Powell without cause would be legally questionable. The report did not establish an exact date or a policy demand attached to the legal review.

USA.title: Trump muses about firing Powell
USA.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump reportedly mused about firing Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell before White House officials explored a possible demotion in February 2019. No specific occasion, exact date or accompanying policy demand was established for Trump's remarks. The subsequent legal review reportedly concluded that firing Powell without cause would be questionable.

USA.title: Trump leaves Powell demotion open ahead of Fed decision
USA.summary: Asked whether he still wanted Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell demoted, President Donald Trump replied, “Let's see what he does,” leaving that prospect open ahead of the Fed's policy announcement. Trump contrasted the Fed's stance with Mario Draghi's signals of European monetary easing and said he wanted a level playing field that he had not received, pressing for more accommodative Fed policy.

USA.title: Trump says Powell made multiple interest-rate mistakes
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump criticized Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for making multiple interest-rate mistakes, referring to increases after Trump became president. Trump argued that the economy was doing well and rates therefore did not need to rise. The June 19, 2019 discussions described his statement as recent but did not establish its exact date.

USA.title: Trump asks White House counsel to examine demoting Powell
USA.summary: President Donald Trump reportedly asked White House legal counsel to examine whether he could demote Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell. The June 19 report linked the inquiry to concerns heard after the Fed’s December rate increase, but did not establish its exact date or a specific policy demand. Counsel reportedly concluded Trump could not demote Powell, while the White House denied the reported suggestion. At his June 19 press conference, Powell said he intended to serve his four-year term and emphasized the Fed’s independence.

USA.title: Trump attacks Fed over last year's rate increases
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump attacked the Federal Reserve on Twitter for raising interest rates too quickly in 2018. The following day, at the Council on Foreign Relations, Fed Chair Jay Powell defended the central bank's independence from short-term political pressure while reinforcing expectations of a July rate cut.

USA.title: Trump says Fed hindered US trade-war position
USA.summary: Speaking on the occasion of the weekend US-China trade truce, President Donald Trump accused the Federal Reserve of hindering the United States' trade-war position. He said, "We're not playing on a fair field" and "The Fed has not been of help to us at all," while claiming the United States was winning despite the central bank. The July 1 report does not establish the precise day of his remarks or an explicit policy demand.

USA.title: Trump announces Shelton and Waller nominations to Fed Board
USA.summary: President Donald Trump announced plans to nominate Judy Shelton and Christopher Waller to the Federal Reserve Board, subject to Senate confirmation. Shelton, his former campaign economic adviser, had criticized the Fed’s authority over markets and questioned its role in setting interest rates; Waller was research director at the St. Louis Fed. Reporting described the nominees as dovish, but the announcement contained no explicit policy demand or threat.

USA.title: Shelton attacks Fed authority and interest-rate setting
USA.summary: Judy Shelton, a US representative on the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development board and former Trump campaign economic adviser, attacked the Federal Reserve as wielding undemocratic, Soviet-style power over markets and suggested it should not set interest rates. The remarks were reported as President Trump announced plans to nominate her to the Fed board; their original occasion and date were not specified.

USA.title: Trump urges US to match Chinese and EU monetary easing
USA.summary: President Donald Trump urged the United States in a tweet to match China and the EU in pumping money into their economies, pressing the Federal Reserve toward monetary easing. He alleged that Beijing and Brussels were manipulating their currencies. The intervention included no explicit threat to Fed officials or institutional autonomy.

USA.title: Trump tells reporters the Fed should cut rates
USA.summary: Speaking to reporters at the end of the weekend, US President Donald Trump urged the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates, saying it would do so if it knew what it was doing. His criticism followed strong June payroll figures showing 224,000 additional jobs, which had reduced pressure for a July rate cut.

USA.title: Maxine Waters presses Powell to resist presidential dismissal
USA.summary: At a House Financial Services Committee hearing, Chairwoman Maxine Waters repeatedly pressed Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell to affirm that he would not leave office if President Trump told him he was fired. She encouraged him to state his refusal clearly. Powell said he would not leave and intended to serve his four-year term. Waters did not advocate a monetary policy direction or threaten his tenure.

USA.title: David Scott pledges support for Powell against presidential pressure
USA.summary: During Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell's appearance before the House Financial Services Committee, Congressman David Scott of Georgia pledged support amid discussion of presidential criticism and possible dismissal, saying, "We will support you. We've got your back in this situation." Scott advocated no specific monetary policy and made no threat.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Fed rates and tightening in tweet
USA.summary: In a tweet on the morning of July 15, 2019, US President Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve's "antiquated policy of rates and tightening," saying the economy was doing great despite it. His criticism favored looser policy and came as Chair Jerome Powell's remarks had heightened expectations of a July rate cut.

USA.title: Ocasio-Cortez challenges Fed unemployment estimates
USA.summary: During congressional testimony, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez questioned whether the Federal Reserve had overestimated the lowest sustainable unemployment rate, given low unemployment without accelerating inflation. Chair Jerome Powell agreed that the sustainable rate was substantially lower than previously thought. The linked report describes the exchange as recent but provides no exact testimony date.

USA.title: Trump tweets that a small Fed cut is insufficient
USA.summary: Ahead of the Federal Reserve's July 31 rate decision, US President Donald Trump tweeted that a small interest-rate cut would not be enough and that the Fed had made all the wrong moves. He demanded a larger cut as the bank was widely expected to reduce rates by 25 basis points, its first cut since 2008.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Fed rate increases in CNBC interview
USA.summary: In a July 2018 CNBC interview, US President Donald Trump expressed disagreement with the Federal Reserve's interest-rate increases, saying he was "not thrilled." Although he described his appointee to lead the Fed, Jerome Powell, as a "very good man," he opposed the rate increases. The linked account does not establish the interview's exact date.

USA.title: Trump objects to Fed rate increase at the UN
USA.summary: Speaking at the United Nations in September 2018, President Donald Trump expressed dissatisfaction with the Federal Reserve's latest interest-rate increase, saying it had raised rates because the economy was doing so well. His remarks opposed the increase but included no threat or attack on the Fed's competence. The linked story does not establish the exact day.

USA.title: Trump calls Fed tightening crazy and loco
USA.summary: In public remarks replayed in a July 31, 2019 report, President Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve for excessively tight policy, saying it was making a mistake, had gone “crazy” and was “going loco.” He expressed unhappiness with its actions and said there was no reason for them, advocating less tightening. The report does not establish the remarks’ precise date or occasion.

USA.title: Trump attacks the Fed's thinking
USA.summary: In a statement recalled in a July 31, 2019 report, US President Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve's judgment, saying it “doesn't get it” and “has faulty thinking.” The report did not identify the statement's occasion or date, and the quoted remarks contained no specific policy demand or threat.

USA.title: Trump asks advisers about replacing Powell
USA.summary: Shortly before Christmas in December 2018, President Donald Trump, angry about Federal Reserve policy and opposed to its interest-rate increases, asked advisers whether he could replace Chair Jerome Powell. Advisers told him he could not fire Powell. The report does not establish the exact date. Powell later told Congress that the law gave him a four-year term and that he intended to serve it.

USA.title: Johnson pressures Fed chair at Texas ranch
USA.summary: President Lyndon Johnson summoned the Federal Reserve chair to his Texas ranch and drove him around at high speeds, according to a historical account. Johnson reportedly later pushed the chair against a wall and accused him of withholding needed money while American soldiers died in Vietnam. Johnson opposed higher borrowing costs that would make the war more expensive. The account does not establish the encounter's exact date.

USA.title: Johnson seeks legal opinion on replacing Fed chair
USA.summary: During the Vietnam War, President Lyndon Johnson asked his Attorney General for a legal opinion on whether he could replace the Federal Reserve chair, amid concerns that higher borrowing costs would increase war expenses and deficits. The Justice Department advised that he could not. The linked account does not establish the date of this request.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Powell after quarter-point rate cut
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump criticized Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell on Twitter after the Fed cut rates by a quarter-point to 2.0–2.25 percent. Trump advocated further easing to keep pace with Europe and China, complaining, “As usual, Powell let us down.” Powell described the cut as a mid-cycle adjustment rather than the start of an extended easing cycle, while clarifying that he was not ruling out additional cuts.

USA.title: Trump tariff announcement described as pressure for further Fed cuts
USA.summary: President Donald Trump announced a 10% tariff on a further $300 billion of Chinese imports, effective September 1. In Bloomberg's August 2 broadcast, CCLA Investment Management CIO James Bevan characterized the announcement as another shot across the Federal Reserve's bow aimed at inducing further rate cuts after its quarter-point cut and restrained guidance on additional easing. This characterization was Bevan's interpretation, not an explicitly stated Fed-related purpose in Trump's announcement.

USA.title: Navarro calls Fed biggest obstacle to growth
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump's top trade adviser, Peter Navarro, called the Federal Reserve the single biggest obstacle to strong US economic growth, blaming it for restraining economic performance. The report did not specify a policy demand or any threat against the bank or its officials.

USA.title: Trump demands substantial Fed rate cuts
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump urged the Federal Reserve to cut interest rates by at least one percentage point and resume quantitative easing, criticizing Chair Jay Powell and the Fed for a “horrendous lack of vision.” He argued that easing would quickly strengthen the global economy and complained about the strong dollar. The demands came amid recession concerns and reported White House consideration of a temporary payroll-tax cut. Boston Fed President Eric Rosengren argued that US economic conditions did not justify further easing. The linked reports provide conflicting timing for Trump's remarks.

USA.title: Trump says Fed should do its job to boost growth
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve for not doing its job, saying its action could produce a tremendous spurt of growth. Rejecting recession concerns, he said the country was far from recession and accused some media figures of wanting one. His remarks pressed the Fed to support stronger growth without specifying a policy instrument or threatening institutional changes.

USA.title: Trump tweet likens Powell to a golfer unable to putt
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump attacked Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell in a newly reported tweet, comparing him to a poor golfer unable to sink a putt despite standing close to the hole. The broadcasts described the comparison as an attack on Powell’s competence but reported no explicit policy demand or threat in this intervention.

USA.title: Trump asks where the Fed is after market moves
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump reacted to financial-market moves by asking, "Where is the Fed?" The remark challenged the Federal Reserve's response ahead of Chair Jay Powell's Jackson Hole speech, without specifying a policy action or making a threat.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Powell and demands a one-percentage-point rate cut
USA.summary: Ahead of Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell’s Jackson Hole speech, President Donald Trump said Powell was doing a very poor job and called for a one-percentage-point interest-rate cut, compared with the quarter-point reduction already delivered. Linked coverage also recalled Trump’s tweeted demand for 100 basis points of easing.

USA.title: Trump questions whether Powell or Xi is the bigger enemy
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump blamed the Federal Reserve and asked whether Fed Chair Jerome Powell or Chinese President Xi Jinping was the bigger enemy. The remarks were recalled in discussions of escalating US-China trade tensions and Powell’s Jackson Hole comments. This intervention attacked Powell without specifying a policy demand or threatening removal or institutional change. The reports do not establish its exact date, with one recalling Thursday or Friday before August 26.

USA.title: Trump says Fed cannot keep up with competition
USA.summary: Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve's competence, saying it “cannot mentally keep up with the competition.” His statement was quoted during a Bloomberg interview about the Fed's next policy steps. The quoted remarks did not specify a policy demand or threaten institutional changes or officials' tenure.

USA.title: Warren proposes Fed instant payments network
USA.summary: In her Wall Street reform package, Elizabeth Warren highlighted delays in clearing paychecks and joined other lawmakers in proposing that the Federal Reserve provide an instant payments network. The proposal sought to give workers immediate access to their earnings. Banks objected that they already offered an instant payments system.

USA.title: Trump blames Fed for inverted yield curve
USA.summary: In a tweet responding to an inversion of the US yield curve, President Donald Trump blamed the Federal Reserve rather than China for economic difficulties. He accused the Fed of raising interest rates too much and too quickly and then cutting them too slowly, called Chair Jerome Powell clueless, and claimed the Fed was holding back American economic gains. The linked report retrospectively discusses the summer episode without establishing the tweet’s exact date.

USA.title: Trump mocks Powell in Friday morning tweet
USA.summary: President Donald Trump mocked Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell in a Friday morning tweet, asking, "Where did I find this Jerome guy anyway?" The criticism reflected his dissatisfaction with Powell and desire for more aggressive interest-rate cuts. Asked about the mockery later that day in Zurich, Powell avoided a personal response and said the Fed would do its job.

USA.title: Trump calls for Fed rates below zero
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump urged the Federal Reserve to take interest rates below zero, according to a September 12 broadcast describing his comments the previous day. Linked coverage also recalled his recent use of “bonehead” to disparage Fed Chair Jerome Powell. His demand sought substantially looser monetary policy, including negative rates like those in Europe.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Fed meeting outcome on Twitter
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump criticized the Federal Reserve on Twitter after its quarter-point rate cut to 1.75–2 percent and signals that no further cuts were forthcoming. Trump, who had been pressing for more aggressive easing, accused Fed chair Jerome Powell of lacking “guts.”

USA.title: Trump demands a rate cut and threatens to dismiss Fed chair
USA.summary: Commentary published on October 28 and 29 reported that US President Donald Trump demanded another Federal Reserve interest-rate cut and indirectly threatened to dismiss its chair if the bank did not comply. The commentators linked his demand to expectations of a further cut and optimism in US equity markets, reporting that Trump wanted stronger economic and stock-market growth. The stories did not date his statement; October 28 is the earliest linked publication date.

USA.title: Trump urges negative rates in Economic Club of New York speech
USA.summary: Speaking at the Economic Club of New York, US President Donald Trump accused the Federal Reserve of harming the economy and putting the country at a competitive disadvantage by not following other central banks into negative interest rates. Describing borrowers being paid under negative rates, he said, “Give me some of that money,” and complained that the Fed would not allow it.

USA.title: Trump presses Powell over high rates at White House meeting
USA.summary: President Donald Trump pressed Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell for lower interest rates at their second White House meeting of the year. In subsequent tweets, Trump described the meeting as cordial but said he had protested that US rates were too high relative to competitor countries. Discussions covered low inflation and dollar strength, with negative rates reportedly also discussed. The Fed said Powell offered no policy expectations beyond stressing that decisions would depend on incoming economic information.

USA.title: Trump links Brazil and Argentina tariffs to criticism of Fed
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump linked criticism of the Federal Reserve to his announcement reinstating steel and aluminium tariffs on Brazil and Argentina. He alleged that their currency devaluations disadvantaged US farmers. The reports described this as his first explicit linkage of tariffs, Fed action and currencies, but did not establish a specific policy demand directed at the Fed in this intervention.

USA.title: Trump demands Fed rate cut and threatens chair's dismissal
USA.summary: In a Norwegian broadcast discussion of the Federal Reserve’s impending rate decision and the 2020 outlook, a participant recalled US President Donald Trump demanding interest-rate cuts and threatening to fire the Fed chair if they did not occur. The linked reports do not establish when or on what occasion Trump made that statement. Participants stressed that Trump did not dictate Fed decisions and noted legal constraints on dismissal.

USA.title: Pressley questions Fed's full-employment responsibility
USA.summary: During Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell’s testimony before the House Financial Services Committee, Massachusetts Democratic Representative Ayanna Pressley asked whether the Fed could ensure economic conditions providing a job for everyone willing and able to work, challenging its fulfillment of the maximum-employment mandate. Powell said the Fed would never declare that goal accomplished, while acknowledging progress. No specific monetary-policy change or threat was reported.

USA.title: Trump criticizes Powell's slow coronavirus response
USA.summary: In a Monday tweet, US President Donald Trump criticized Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell for being slow to act despite the Fed's willingness to cut interest rates. The criticism favored faster easing amid administration discussions of an emergency Fed rate cut and a possible tax cut to contain the economic and market fallout from coronavirus.

USA.title: Trump calls Fed emergency rate cut too small
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump reacted on Twitter to the Federal Reserve’s emergency 50-basis-point interest-rate cut, calling it far too small and demanding further reductions. He criticized the Fed for lagging behind rather than getting ahead as it responded to economic risks from the coronavirus outbreak. The cut was its first between scheduled meetings since 2008.

USA.title: Trump urges Treasury secretary to press Powell for more radical easing
USA.summary: During a Monday meeting, US President Donald Trump urged Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin to press Federal Reserve Chair Jerome H. Powell for more radical monetary easing amid the coronavirus crisis. Trump also said Powell should never have been appointed and was harming the country and his presidency.

USA.title: Trump endorses Fed emergency rate cut
USA.summary: Speaking minutes after the Federal Reserve announced an emergency rate cut to near zero and at least $700 billion in additional bond purchases amid the coronavirus outbreak, President Donald Trump said the measures made him very happy and congratulated the Fed for lowering rates. His remarks endorsed easing without expressing criticism, further demands or threats.

USA.title: Trump thanks Powell for coronavirus response
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump said he had called Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell to thank him for efforts to counter the coronavirus-driven economic slowdown. The report noted the Fed's move to directly finance US companies. Trump's remarks expressed appreciation without an explicit policy demand, criticism or threat.

USA.title: Trump urges Fed to adopt negative rates
USA.summary: US President Donald Trump suggested that the Federal Reserve adopt negative interest rates. Coverage reported that Fed Chair Jerome Powell rejected the suggestion while urging Congress and the White House to provide additional fiscal stimulus.

USA.title: Warren urges tighter restrictions on emergency lending recipients
USA.summary: At a Senate Banking Committee hearing on pandemic relief, Senator Elizabeth Warren urged additional restrictions on companies receiving Federal Reserve–Treasury emergency loans, including executive compensation limits. She argued that taxpayer assistance should not fund executive bonuses. Treasury Secretary Stephen Mnuchin responded that Congress had not agreed to those restrictions and that imposing them was not Treasury's responsibility.

USA.title: Senators press Powell and Mnuchin on additional state aid
USA.summary: At a Senate Banking Committee hearing on the pandemic response, senators pressed Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell and Treasury Secretary Stephen Mnuchin on whether additional assistance to states would be appropriate to prevent long-term economic damage if the downturn continued through 2020 or into 2021. The report identifies no related threats or accusations.

USA.title: Kudlow criticizes Powell's economic assessment as overly negative
USA.summary: White House economic adviser Larry Kudlow criticized Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell’s economic assessment as overly negative after the Fed delivered a downbeat outlook and signaled that rates would probably remain near zero through 2022. The report identified no specific policy demand or threat from Kudlow.

USA.title: Trump nominates Judy Shelton to Federal Reserve Board
USA.summary: President Donald Trump nominated Judy Shelton, a consultant to his 2016 campaign and longtime gold-standard advocate, to the Federal Reserve Board. With Senate confirmation pending, the report described the appointment as a way for Trump to leave his imprint on the Fed before leaving office. It suggested Shelton could dissent and disrupt consensus but would be unlikely to block Fed actions as one governor.

USA.title: Shelton compares Fed monetary policymaking to Soviet planning
USA.summary: Judy Shelton, President Donald Trump's nominee to the Federal Reserve Board and a former consultant to his presidential campaign, compared the Fed's monetary policymaking to Soviet economic planning. The comparison challenged the legitimacy of the Fed's policymaking role without advocating a specific policy direction. The report recalled the comparison as the Senate prepared to consider her confirmation.

USA.title: Mnuchin declines extension of Fed emergency lending programs and requests unused funds
USA.summary: In a letter to Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell, US Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin declined to extend several emergency lending facilities beyond December and requested the return of $455 billion in unused funds for potential congressional spending elsewhere. The facilities supported corporate debt, state and local governments, businesses and asset-backed securities. He argued that markets no longer needed them and that he lacked authority to extend them; the Fed disputed that interpretation and said the facilities should remain as economic backstops. Mnuchin separately requested 90-day extensions for four short-term funding facilities, including those supporting commercial paper and money market mutual funds.

USA.title: Mulvaney challenges Yellen's discussion of inequality
USA.summary: At a congressional hearing in 2015, Republican Congressman Mick Mulvaney challenged Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen's discussion of inequality as political and outside her jurisdiction, urging her to stay within the Fed's remit. Yellen defended discussing major economic trends and problems as consistent with her predecessors' practice. The linked retrospective does not establish the hearing's exact date.

USA.title: Trump declines to renominate Yellen as Fed chair
USA.summary: President Donald Trump declined to nominate Janet Yellen for a second term as Federal Reserve chair despite economic expansion during her tenure. Sources told The Wall Street Journal that Trump had suggested her short stature was one concern; the White House declined to comment. The retrospective account establishes neither a monetary-policy demand nor the date of the non-renewal decision.

USA.title: Warren and Brown warn against extending bank capital relief
USA.summary: In a letter seen by the Financial Times, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Sherrod Brown urged the Federal Reserve and other US regulators not to extend looser bank capital requirements introduced at the start of the pandemic. They argued that the relief had created new economic risks and that extending it would be a grave error. Banks said allowing the relief to expire would make trading US government debt and extending credit more difficult.

USA.title: Yellen suggests rates may need to rise to prevent overheating
USA.summary: At an Atlantic conference discussing the sustainability of the Biden administration’s stimulus, Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said interest rates might need to rise to prevent the US economy from overheating. Her remarks contrasted with Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell’s guidance and reportedly exacerbated a technology-stock sell-off. Later that day, at a Wall Street Journal event, she clarified that she was neither predicting nor recommending a rate increase.

USA.title: Yellen welcomes higher Fed rates as a benefit
USA.summary: U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen welcomed the prospect of higher Federal Reserve interest rates if President Biden's stimulus plan prompted them, saying this would benefit the Fed and society. In comments reported alongside the G7 tax agreement, she said inflation and interest rates had been too low for too long and welcomed a return toward normal levels.

USA.title: Lawmakers challenge Powell over inflation complacency
USA.summary: Republican and Democratic US lawmakers pressed Federal Reserve Chair Jay Powell about inflation during his congressional appearance, following unexpectedly strong June consumer-price data. Powell rejected criticism that the Fed was too complacent, reiterated that price increases were temporary and said the bank was ready to act if necessary to bring inflation down.

USA.title: Trump replaces Yellen with Powell to shift regulatory leadership
USA.summary: In 2017, President Donald Trump declined to offer Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen a second term and selected Fed Governor Jerome Powell instead. The retrospective report describes Trump as seeking a Republican with a softer approach to bank regulation while preserving market stability through Powell’s monetary-policy continuity with Yellen.
